utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Are you ready to continue, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Good morning to everybody. Good morning to Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Theunens, I would like it remind you hopefully for the last time that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you will remember, Mr. Theunens, we showed you the order by General Cervenko concerning the role of the special MUP forces in Operation Storm, as the result of which or, rather, the order itself envisages two stages upon the completion of which another order would be issued and that the units of the special police had to be prepared for that other operation that is to follow. I hope you remember that. Let us take a look at what happens after the special police units have carried out their assignments several days later. Let's look at D550, please. Soon we will see document D550, which is an order for the continuation of combat activities at D plus 1. This is an order by General Cervenko. I suppose you had occasion to see just now on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I have also seen it before, but I'm not sure whether it is included in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Whether it is or not, let us look at item 2 of the order, which states that combat activities are to be continued at an intensified pace. What they are trying to indicate is that they want to ensure accelerated advancement of the units. Would you agree with me on that? Not only of those units but of the other forces involved in Operation Storm as well. The dynamics, the dynamic pace, is something that is being insisted upon. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't necessarily draw the same conclusion. General Cervenko, at least in paragraph 2, simply orders to continue the combat activities and intensify them. But I think if we go further to the order and maybe if we see that deadlines are imposed to fulfil or to reach certain objectives, that would give us a better indication as to whether or not General Cervenko wants to have combat activities or the tempo accelerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. A question on that score which falls within your expertise. Can you explain to us in a couple of sentences why in this type of combat when advancement is made toward the enemy and the first line of defence is being broken, why is it important to maintain the pace -- the achieved pace of advancement?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason is what you want to keep the momentum, i.e., the attacking force has obtained the initiative because they managed to breach the first line of the enemy. And now before the enemy can prepare some kind of a counteraction or counterattack, it is important that the attacking forces maintain the momentum and prevent the enemy from reorganizing and preparing any kind of counter-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have D552 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we're about to see, Mr. Theunens, is the order for the continuation of combat activities on day D plus 2 also issued by the chief of the General Staff, General Cervenko, which envisages operations to take place on D plus 2. In item 1, we can see that the order concerns the Split Military District. It says that the general areas of Otric and Srb need to be seized and the state border -- one needs to come out on the state border. Let us take a look at part 2 of your report, specifically page 285. At least that's page in my copy. We realized yesterday we had different enumerations. The date I mentioned is the 7th of August and I'm referring to item 4. Have you found that portion where you say that the special police forces captured Mazin and Srb? From the order we have on our screens, it follows that it was not the task of the special police units to capture Srb; rather, it was the task given to the Split Military District. You base your conclusion on document 65 ter 00317. Can we therefore have the document called up, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it's on English page 281, I think the copy I'm using and the others are using.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm using an English text, and it is page 285, so it is a different version. But any way you found it in your material?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're referring in footnote 1153 to document 65 ter 00317. And you say that this is the war path of the Ministry of Interior of the Sibenik special police unit?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And more specifically, I found it on English page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could we have English page 20, please, on the screen, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So what we see -- [Interpretation] What we can see on our screens is the translation of a newspaper article wherein it -- wherein it is stated that the units of the special police liberated the -- Srb. Mr. Theunens, I'm somewhat surprised by the fact that in your expert report you should be referring to daily newspaper articles as credible sources. Isn't that a bit odd in view of the documentation you had at your disposal to review?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I mean, open sources can be an important source of information. I think it is not just a newspaper article. This is a newspaper article that is included in an official document published by the Sibenik special police unit called war path of MUP special police unit Sibenik, so my understanding was that if the Sibenik special police unit includes this in its official history of its activities, then there must be a good reason for that. And from the methodology point of view that would increase, in my view, the reliability of this particular source for -- in this context, i.e., the reliability of the press source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Theunens, newspapers as the source at the base of your expertise regardless of what you say, to me, does not seem reliable or credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at D554, shall we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, looking at the last sentence it was comment that you do not consider newspapers to be reliable, which is fine with me, but to say, Regardless what you say, I find newspapers unreliable. Where the witness explained why in these specific circumstances, he considered this not just to be newspaper article is a kind of comment and not very fair to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My position to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you say, Regardless what you say. And give your own opinion is not really what assists the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see D554, which is the summary report on the execution of Operation Oluja, Storm, which is the -- which is an official document. Have you seen this document before? This is the official document from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia issued by the chief of the Main Staff, General Zvonimir Cervenko. If we turn to page 3 of the document for the date of the 8th of August, we shall see that it is stated therein that the forces of the Split Military District liberated Srb. In other words, by no means did the specialists from the Ministry of Interior liberate Srb. Do you agree, Mr. Theunens, that this official document from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia makes statements that are different from the newspaper articles you referred to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just for your information, I have included this document, D554, for example, on English page 131, and, indeed, there is an inconsistency in relation as to who captured or took control over Srb. I must say I had not paid attention to that before and, indeed, if there would be a specific analysis about who took Srb when, the different source would say have to be compared and then we would try to find other sources in order to determine what exactly happened and who took Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the document we just had on our screens - that's D552 - the order by General Cervenko to continue combat activities on D plus 2. And can we turn to page 2 of the document. I'm interested in item 3. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... that would be the third page in English version, please. Yes, yes, thank you thank you it's okay. Count 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This particular item of the order of General Cervenko gives assignments to the members of the MUP, and it says: "Upon capturing the Bruvno and Malovan saddles continue the attack towards Donji Lapac and capture this area in -- with the participation of the forces of the Gospic Military District on the left flank and the forces of the Split Military District on the right flank. Mr. Theunens, it is without any doubt that the chief of the Main Staff of the HV in command of Operation Storm issued assignments to members of the special police. I'm highlighting this particular fact against the cases put forward in your report at page 281 of my copy - that's item 9, under the date of the 5th of August - day two, in other words, 1995. I'll quote your report where you say: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... first two days of operation the SJP command decides to initiate the third stage." [Interpretation] In view of your experience and capacity of a military expert, is it possible to conclude that in the continuation of combat activities, a decision was taken in the command of the special police and not at the Main Staff which was in charge of the operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to reply. My reply would consist of two components. The first component can be found on English page 295 in my version, under the title: 4, command and control and communications procedure over the special police during Operation Oluja --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Theunens, but my question was very simple.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm trying to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Please do.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there I state command and control, Mladen Markac, command of the SUP doing operation Storm is subordinated to the chief of the HV Main Staff and keeps him informed of the operations conducted by the SUP. So that is one important element. I will read it out again for the transcript. Mladen Markac commander of the SUP doing operation storm is subordinated to the chief of the HV Main Staff. Now the excerpt you took from my report is based on Exhibit P614 where I copied the text of this document, whereby P614 is an official document of the special police sector. It's the analysis of progress of Operation Storm. So when you read out this section from my report, obviously it has to be considered in the overall context where I clearly state that the special police, i.e., Colonel General Mladen Markac and subordinated to him the chief of the special police sector received their orders from the chief of the Main Staff, General Zvonimir Cervenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for area answer, Mr. Theunens, but this was not answer to my question. My question was: Have you ever experienced in your expertise that the lawyer level of command has been reached their own decision to continue with a combat operation, apart from the higher command?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initiative is an important aspect of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is not initiative; it's a decision. Because you said, Command decides.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, initiative is not decision, but decisions sometimes result in decisions, so, therefore, if the witness -- let's give him a fair chance to answer the question. And as far as the question is concerned, apparently you are not seeking a comment on the situation in Croatia at that time but, rather, in more general terms. If you would clearly put that to the witness, there's a better chance that he'll understand your question. Mr. Theunens, the question is not about the situation in August 1995 in Croatia but in more general terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Without going into too great details, initiative is one of important or key qualities for military leaders at all levels. Of course, initiative has to fit, if I can express myself in that way, in the overall concept, i.e., the orders of the superior, and again coming back to what you quoted in my report from my report, it is stated, indeed, that the SJP command decides to initiative the third stage of the operation with the approval of the HV Main Staff. And this is actually what initiative is about and how, then, initiative can result in a decision, obviously with the approval of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Mr. Theunens, but my position is just opposite, vice versa. Okay, but we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have D322.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, we will be looking at order -- at an order for D plus 3, also issued by the chief of the Main Staff, General Zvonimir Cervenko, for the continuation of combat activities, which, again, calls for an energetic advancement. It asks for the troops to come out on the borders, and it also says that the Split and Gospic Military District Commanders have to coordinate with the commander of the special police units of the MUP, the times of the attacks to take place along the designated axes. Can we have your comment on this, or is the order, in fact, a logical continuation of the combat activities carried out hither to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, it is it a logical continuation of the earlier orders and the earlier combat operations. General Cervenko orders to reach the border as soon as possible. And, of course, as units of the special police are operating on the -- on the boundary between the zone of responsibility of the Gospic Military District in the north and the Split Military District in the south, it is -- it is essential to ensure coordination between these three groups of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I would like to direct your attention to part two of your report; in other words, for the 4th of August 1995. In my copy that is page 278, and the paragraph is number 4. Please alert me when you find the paragraph. It starts with the word "Markac." Mr. Theunens, I would like you to look at the portion of the paragraph where you state that at 1132 hours Markac reported on the artillery fire against his forces from Medak. In the brackets you state that this was friendly fire. Can you tell us what is your source for the statement that this was friendly fire?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we see the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would refer to the document P614, please, and page 8.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I'm quoting from D555. The war diary of the HV Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will come to it, Mr. Theunens. So it is page 8 of the P614, and I would like to draw your attention to 1215.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the English page that will be the previous page, right, and 1215 is a time that I'm interested in. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, look at the relevant portion of the document, which analyses the course of Operation Storm and which was sent to the Main Staff of the Croatian army from the special police. Let us look at the entry for the relevant time, where it says that the enemy opened artillery fire from Medak upon Marasovac. My conclusion, therefore, is that this was not friendly fire; it was enemy fire. [In English] You cited in your report, and this is D555.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, you're right, and it also states at 2000 on the same page that Medak is liberated by SJP by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The second day 5th of August, 2000?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is footnote 1122 in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to see the document D555, and that will be in the English version page 19. [Interpretation] What we are going to see is the war diary kept at the Main Staff where entries were made from the field during Operation Storm. I believe you did have an opportunity to see this war diary, did it you not, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I have quoted from it, the incident of the artillery fire is footnote 1098, in part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I would like to draw your attention to the number 139.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I drew the wrong conclusion at the time when I wrote this report, that, at the time of the artillery fire, Medak was already taken by Croatian forces, which we have seen now is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have 65 ter 1026, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the document, Mr. Theunens, I wanted to ask you this: You have come across certain documents in which General Cervenko, the chief of the Main Staff, reported the president, Dr. Tudjman on the course of Operation Storm. President Tudjman was also the supreme commander of the armed forces. This is one such report for the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I have come across such reports, and I have included a number of them in section 2 of part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2 of the document in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We are about to see page 2. Mention is made there of the special forces of the MUP after having take Malovan and Bruvno continued their combat and linked up with the forces of the Military District of Gospic in the area of Udbina. The other portion of the special forces with the artillery support of the Military District Gospic took over Gornji and Donji Lapac. The third portion of the forces were at the passes of Malovan and Otric. These facts are known to you from the documents that you saw. Is that correct, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And I believe it's largely coherent with the reports of the special police both the analysis P614 as well as reports by special police units on the events of -- and the operations of the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just been reminded from my case manager that I didn't apply for an introducing into the evidence 65 ter 00317, which is a news article, so I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the reason why I consulted with my colleagues is because having media stuff into evidence always causes the Chamber to -- to consider that, but in view of the answers of this witness, that this document was attached to a report, and we heard no further questions about it so apparently it is not challenged. The Chamber has no difficulty in those circumstances to immediately decide and to admit into evidence and D1098.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I tender into the evidence as well 65 ter 01026, which is on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1099, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1099 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar, could I have on the screen, please, P585, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document we are about to see is a report by Colonel General Mladen Markac. It actually came from the Ministry of Interior and the head of special forces to the chief of Main Staff on the lines reached by the special police joint forces. I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 3 in which it is stated that the forces of the special police were mopping up the terrain at the foot of Mount Velebit with an aim to destroy the enemy groups that may have been left behind. In the documents of the special police that refer to mopping up such as this one, and we will see some others, the term used is destruction of the leftover enemy or sabotage terrorist groups. Do you agree with me that that term was used in the reports of the special police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is for sure one of the terms that is being used. And it is most often used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I would like to see a P577, please. [Interpretation] And this document, as we will see, there are tables which were made to complement the MUP special forces reports on the mopping up of the terrain you referred to those in the second part of your report, page 288, I'm referring to the 9th of August. It is the last entry in paragraph 3. In your report, you mentioned the term "liquidated" as the term used to identify those members of the enemy forces that were killed during the mopping up operation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, search operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, if we look at the table in exhibit 577 for the 23rd of August, the ERN number is 06092942, we see there in the column liquidated that the special police forces from the Split-Dalmatia county registered three persons that had been liquidated. Do you see that, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see, and this is also --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in my report on page 284 for the other page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to deal with this issue because I take issue with this term, "liquidated," when reviewing the reports sent by General Markac to the Main Staff, I did not come across a term, not once. My question is this: Do you know who made these tables that can be found in Exhibit P577? It is obvious that this some sort of statistics concerning the reports that were submitted by the special police to the Main Staff. Do you know who was the author of those tables? And I would also like to draw your attention to the last page in the stamp. It says that this document came from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I only see the English in front of me. But if it is a form used, because maybe the stamp is just kind of a stamp for the archives or something that was put on it afterwards as I've seen on many other document. Documents that were provided to OTP and that originated from archives in state archives in Croatia often had stamps, where I had the impression the stamp was put on the document at a later stage. Unfortunately, I cannot really read -- I can see 25/04, but then on my screen, I cannot read the year. Any way, it says 2007. Well, sorry I didn't notice that, so it was a stamp probably that was put on the document afterwards, and which has to do with archiving. I was under the understanding this was a form that was used by the special police sector, i.e., that had been prepared by special police sector without any particular author being known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to put the following to you, Mr. Theunens. In the reports of the special police the term "liquidated" or to liquidate was never used. Let us have a look at the reports that refers to the 23rd of April -- of August, in which we have the table stating that three people were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic should not overlap and wait for the end of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you are invited not to overlap and to wait until the translation is finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is my problem, Your Honour. I try to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So I was asking for 65 ter 2463, please, Mr. Registrar. Could we go on page 2 in English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, this is a report of the special police on the search of terrain that was sent to General Cervenko at the Main Staff, referring to the 23rd, and that is the date for which the tables state that three people were liquidated. In item 3, we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have a wrong document on the screen, but I believe previously we have a right one. So I repeat, it is 65 ter 2463, page 2. That's the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 3 in the last sentence it says: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... terrorist group (three armed military conscripts) was destroyed in Sipkovac." [Interpretation] That was the term used in the report of the special police which is different from the term used in the summary reports, that is to say, the tables. That is obvious, is it not? There is no mention of the term "liquidated," rather, the military term is used, stating that the terrorist group was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we see that the term "destroyed" is being used here, whereas in other occasion in official form, the term "liquidated" is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In the reports of the special police units, could you show me one document of that kind. In the meantime could I tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1100 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But to save some time, Mr. Theunens, it is my statement the wording "liquidated" is never used in the official reports of the special police. In the meantime during the break, if you could find one, I would be happy to see it.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't need more time. As I put it in the report on page 283, I said, A form, and then between quotation marks, "report by the MUP special police sector" uses the expression liquidated to identify members of the enemy force who have been search in [indiscernible] operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The point seems to be clear. Mr. Mikulicic finds it important to emphasise that that word is not used in any report that it could be identified as coming from the special police. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, the next question I have has to do with artillery support received by the special police in its advancement during Operation Storm. In the documents you referred to and that I reviewed, the term "artillery support" is used. Can you explain in the military sense of the word, what does it actually mean, artillery support?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the official term should be fire support, but fire support can consist of artillery, close air support, as well as the use of mortars. I use the concept artillery support, because I only address the use of weapons qualified as artillery, i.e., cannons, Howitzers, and multiple-barrel rocket launchers which are used to provide fire support to the troops that are conducting a manoeuvre. For example, if they carry out an attack, an attack is traditionally described as a combination of fire and movement. The troops that are moving, they can also -- they will also use fire, but, of course, there are certain limitations to their compatibilities. And that's why artillery, which will be static will be called in to provide additional support against the enemy in order to facilitate the attack or the manoeuvre of the manoeuvring forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This artillery support to the units of special police was provided by HV forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is a combination. The special police has -- it has its own artillery assets, and at the same time, there is, first of all, artillery support being provided by HV units as well as examples of individual artillery weapons being made available to special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you come across an example, in which HV forces resubordinated; that is to say, placed certain resources of theirs under the command of the special police forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to locate the artillery section in the part on special police. It's important to note that the provision of artillery support does not necessarily include subordination. It can happen, but it doesn't have to. Of course it includes coordination because the support has to be provided at the right time in the right location and for the correct duration of time because, otherwise, maybe it will be ineffective or even worse, you will -- I mean, the own forces may be exposed to friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm referring to page 310 of the second part of your report, paragraph 5, which talks about the use of artillery by the special police, and I have item 2 in mind, in which you state that -- well, you cite an example when the Split Military District handed over an artillery piece to the special police. The piece was a Howitzer. Do you see that in your report, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is on page -- in my version, page 306, and it corresponds with footnote 1279. But I understand that we were talking about a battery of Howitzers which is -- in general, six Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And there you refer to a 65 ter document. That is 4555 in footnote 1279. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... 65 ter 4555. [Interpretation] What we are going to see, Mr. Theunens, is something you reviewed when drafting your expert report, is a report by the OG commander, Colonel Mladen Fuzul, the OG Zadar. What is mentioned there is the handing over of a Howitzer battery of 122 millimetres from the OG Zadar to the special police forces. Based on that document, you concluded that the OG Zadar handed over this Howitzer battery to the special forces of the MUP. However, Mr. Theunens, I would like to draw your attention to the introductory part of the order which refers to a document that we will see shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1101 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter 5633.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm going show you, Mr. Theunens, is a document referred to in this order. That is the agreement of the 6th of August, 1995, number 8001/95-02/08. It is clear from this document, Mr. Theunens, that on Mr. Markac's request and in agreement with OG Zadar, the Chief of Staff, General Zvonimir Cervenko, agreed that a 122-millimetre Howitzer battery with ammunition as war booty of the special police should be handed over for use to the command of OG Zadar. Therefore, this is precisely contrary to the situation that you described.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I tender this into the evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, first of all, you were invited to slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to catch time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second, I take it that the question mark on the transcript means that you'd like to hear the comment of the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I was intending to hear from the expert is whether this is a completely opposite situation of that one that he describes in his report, and he admitted it is, so we can go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours, and I apologise for the error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1112, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1112 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Mikulicic, the reason why I was waiting for the answer of the witness is that we exactly at the same time got the invitation for you to slow down, so I missed his answer. But from what he says now, I must take it that he had answered the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And just to add, I must have missed this second document, because the second document explains the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to pull up on the screen P505 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, in your report - in my version, it is page 321 the fifth chapter - where you mention military discipline and alleged serious crimes committed in the area of responsibility during Operation Storm. I would like to assist you to locate that. It is the Roman -- it is item aa, in small letters. I believe it is page 321 in copy. Have you found it, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear Mr. Mikulicic, Your Honour, he is inaudible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I hear that it is difficult for the interpreters to hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I must pay more attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is difficult for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, it's section five of your report which is titled enforcement of the military discipline and so on.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And I'm referring to the paragraph 1. Signed as double small a, aa, which starts with the words: "On 26th August ..." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I think we're talking about a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In my report, it's page 321. And 320, so it has to be minor difference in your version.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So ... labelled as aa. Never mind. What I intend to do is the following: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, you referenced a document which the Prosecution tried to tender into evidence on a couple of occasions, and it was marked 505, and we still haven't heard from Their Honours whether the document will be admitted or not because the Defence challenged its authenticity. Purportedly this is a letter from General Markac to the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, about the letter from Madam Elisabeth Rehn and the reaction to that letter. I would like to tell you, Mr. Theunens, that the Defence does not consider this document to be authentic because of the absence of signature, stamp, or a reference number, such as is normally assigned to every letter. That's why I'm referring to that part of your report, where you mention the disputed document, and I have to challenge that portion of the report because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... regarding this particulars portion of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is on page 411 in the English version. I mean, I'm not familiar with the background. I didn't know it was disputed and whether it was MFI or not. You just state there is no number, but when you look at the Croatian version, it says Boj, above Zagreb, and Boj, in my view, stands --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The portion of the official number is missing.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But it is not up to your expertise. I'm just trying to show that you that this document is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So we could go on. [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, I'd like us to talk about an operation undertaken by special MUP forces and the HV after Operation Storm was concluded. What I have in mind are search operations. First of all, going through the documents when drafting your report, and in order to try and save some time, can we agree without going through all of the documents that the operation of search or mopping up of terrain was conducted by the units of the special police as well as HV units, then military police units, as well as the special units of the police called anti-terrorist platoons. Do you go with this assertion of mine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, and I would like to add that based on the documents that I saw I came to the conclusions that these operations were predominantly conducted by special police units, but as you mentioned also other types of units participated in these clearing operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may we have document 65 ter 2298 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now be looking at a document which came from the HV Main Staff from General Zvonimir Cervenko, who, in this document, orders the forces of MUP to carry out mop-up and fully take out area of Petrova Gora. This document also bears the date of the 10th of August. Do you know, Mr. Theunens, where Petrova Gora is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the fact that you asked the question, and I have also checked in the atlas the position Petrova Gora is. My understanding of the use of Petrova Gora in this context was that we were talking about the area known as Petrova Gora in the zone of Kordun, which is north of Bihac, but I realize that there are different Petrova Goras. However, when I see the document, I see Topusko, Glina, and so on, and that corresponds with that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Theunens. My question is whether you can confirm that that location is outside of borders of former Sector South where Operation Storm took place and it is charged in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the record, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Petrova Gora as included in this order, if it is the one in the Kordun, is outside former Sector South. Kordun was located in former UN Sector North, and this is page 284 in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I tender this documented into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D1103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1103 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you recall, Mr. Theunens, I showed you a document yesterday from 1993 by General Markac in which it is stated what sort of operations the special police was supposed to undertake. In the document, those operations and activities are specified as those which need to be executed during search operations. And it also serves as a definition of the measures undertaken by the special police. Those are searching of the terrain in search of the leftover sabotage terrorist groups, locating the warehouses with ammunition, locating any minefields, and similar activities which form part of a search operation. Do you agree with this assertion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it is also confirmed in D528, i.e., the 1996 brochure which can be found in footnote 381 in part 1 of the report, English page 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. [Interpretation] My next question, though it may seem odd, I will put it any way. Do you believe that the search and clean-up or mop-up operations are quite legitimate operations normally carried out under such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a concept they are part of a military operations, and there are rules and procedures how they conducted, so, indeed, I would consider them by concept legitimate and kind of normal operations. Everything depends, of course, on the manner in which they are conducted, i.e., the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have 65 ter, please, 1386.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the mop-up operations carried out by the special police, the joint forces of the special policemen took place, the ones we referred to yesterday. They were, to remind you, formed from elements of the units of the special police attached to police administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... 65 ter 1386, please. 1386.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certain police administrations set aside a number of their special policemen to take part in search operations. That's beyond any doubt. What I would like to clarify with the help of the document that is show up on our screens a moment ago is in what way was the participation of elements of special policemen from police administrations technically organised, whereas that when they were part of these joint forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The hard copy of this document it is a -- maybe we could go over the ERN numbers. It's a 0605-3079. On my copy, on my hard copy is stamped like it is a ter that I cited but obviously there is some mistake in it. Could we try, then, over the number 0605-3079.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe this is an error in the ERN in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not referring to the document in your report. Obviously, this is a wrong number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the number on the screen bears the number you just gave, 0605-3079. So, therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm a little bit surprised at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think if you go to the last two pages, there is, I think, a different document. Maybe that is it what you are looking for. So pages 2, 3, and 4, if you move on, so it might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for your help, Mr. Waespi. That's the one. So we find it. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, while we're waiting for the English version of the document, I will tell you what it is all about. It has to do with the request of the commander of a special police unit, or, rather, of the unit from the Split-Dalmatia police administration to the accounting service of that administration about the payment of per diems. Do you agree with me that it follows from this document that the units which took part in the mop-up operation, namely, Operation Oluja/Obruc which is mentioned in this document and we discussed it before, were, in fact, financed by their respective police administrations, and in this way they were reliant upon or tied to their respective administrations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, indeed, indicates that members of the special police unit Split-Dalmatia are paid daily allowances for their field service by the police administration Split-Dalmatia. I have not looked into the aspect of the paying of daily allowances, because when I was reviewing documents that covered the aspects of command, control coordination, and, I didn't see any references or any -- yeah, references to the payment of daily allowances. What I mean by that is that the fact that daily allowances are paid by organisation X, Y,or Z, does not have an implication for command, control, coordination, and reporting arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections. Obviously, the first page appears to be out of sequence, but I'm sure we can remove that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first page apparently being page 35 of something and then the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is also different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also -- so I take it, Mr. Mikulicic, what you're seeking to be admitted into evidence is the third and the fourth page of -- is there any way that you could upload these two pages and get rid of the other two? So that we can with focus on what makes sense to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is a document from the Prosecution's 65 ter list. I'm not sure that we, as the Defence, may intervene into documents presented by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see no problem, that if you longer document in which you're interested in a portion of it, that you upload that portion, perhaps not under that same 65 ter number, but under another number, and that we then admit into evidence the relevant portion of that document. Mr. Registrar, pages 3 and 4, of this document, once separately uploaded by the Markac Defence, will receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1104, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1104, once uploaded, will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, I would like to direct your attention to the following document, 65 ter 01085. This is an order by the chief of the Main Staff, General Zvonimir Cervenko, dated the 11th of September, 1995, sent to General Markac, where in it is ordered that by 20 September - I'm referring to item 1 - the Special Forces of the MUP at the strength of some 2.000 men be sent to the southern front, and we can see that what is referred to is Metkovic in that part of the front line. Mr. Theunens, it is indubitable that a 2.000 strong contingent is taken out of their area in which they were engaged up to that point and sent far to the south which is a very long way away from Sector South. Is it not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the southern, as it is translated, the southern theatre of operations in the Metkovic area is the area which is -- I would have to read a map, but I guess it is like 50 kilometres south of Split, southeast of Split. It's the wider area of Dubrovnik, and that is what the order states. Now, I don't know to what extent this order was implemented. I remember from my activities in UNPROFOR that there was, indeed, an increased intention in that area, and that there were redeployments of Croatian forces noticed by UNPROFOR members in the wider Dubrovnik area, but then after a couple of days, it seemed that various units that had been sent were withdrawn, and that, yes, there were no significant operational developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Mr. Theunens. However, what I wanted to demonstrate through this document is that from the area liberated in the course of Operation Storm, pursuant to an order by the Main Staff, 2.000 special policemen were redeployed to area of Croatia that was quite a way away from that area. Do you agree on that score?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order states that they have to be redeployed. However, when you look at English page 294, part 2 of the report, we see that the clearing operations are still conducted, for example, between the 21st and the 29th of September. So it is not clear to what extent this order by General Markac was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm drawing your attention to the fact that this is not General Markac order, rather, this is an order that comes from the chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And it's coherent with what I have explained earlier, that is that the units of the special police prior to, during, and after Operation Storm, are subordinated to the chief of the HV Main Staff, who issues orders along the chain of command through the assistant minister of the interior, Mladen Markac, or Colonel General Mladen Markac, and then further on, to the special police units via the special police sector. So it is coherent with what we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1105, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1105 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For your reference is, Your Honours, in document P621, which is already an exhibit, the exact number of members of the special police is mentioned, the number of those who took part in Operation Storm. For the record, I will state that the number ranges from 1790, that was the head count on the last day of Operation Storm, to 2450, which was their strength on the first day of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I still have a couple of questions left and only on one topic. While preparing your expertise that we've been dealing with for a while now, which material did you study concerning the structure, organisation, purpose, and role of the special police? Did you have an opportunity to come across scientific papers on the issue, or the curricula of the training at the police academy, which had to be taken by the special policemen? Did you have occasion to read scientific papers or articles on the matter?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read articles on the special police. Some of these articles originate from a magazine known as, I think, it was Jane's intelligence review, where there were a number of articles, for example, one by somebody I knew, I mean, from my time in UNPROFOR, and he wrote -- he published under the name Norman Eric, even though it's not his real name. I must say I was also familiar with the special police from my stay in UNTAES mission where we had access to -- okay, these were not scientific articles, but these were military magazines. I was -- I personally discussed with some members of the special police at that time because they were located in a zone -- at least that was in summer 1996 where they were not allowed to be present. Then I have also, of course, the material that is included in my report. There is, for example, P588, which is I agree or admit, a brochure. I have requested during the preparation of my report for more complete documents or more specific documents in relation to the organisation, role, and -- yeah, structure of the special police. One of the documents we obtained was, I believe, it is 65 ter 5031. It has been tendered now, but it's a document with the job descriptions. For example, we had a job description under title 280 of the chief of special police unit. I was very surprised by that document because it was incomplete. There should also have been a job description of the assistant minister of the interior for example --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Mr. Theunens. We are quite short on time. Let me complete this topic, if I understand you correctly, you read several newspaper -- several articles in specialized journals. You spoke to some members of the special police, but you did not conduct specific research at the police academy in Zagreb or read any Ph.D. papers in order to gain specialized knowledge and an insight into the training required in accordance with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, when it comes to the role of an expert witness. Mr. Theunens, it is true, is it not, that if one were to apply scientific criteria and the requirements of this Tribunal that when it comes to the structure, legislation, and the doctrine of use of the units of the special police in times of peace and in combat, you, in fact, do not have specialized knowledge which is required by the ICTY of an expert witness. That's right, is it not, you do not have that specialist knowledge? This is your first case where you appear as an expert witness to testify on the issues of the special police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are a lot of questions included, but I will just answer the last component. I mean for the time being, unless I'm requested to also answer or address other components. It is correct that this is the first case where I have been requested to write a report on the use and activities of special police. However, I consider that, based on my education, training, and experience, I am indeed qualified to address the topics I have addressed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That concludes my cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my questions, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break. We will resume at five minutes to 11.00, but could I have a forecast.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will stick within 15 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which means that the next witness should remain stand by. We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you never know who is hiding from whom, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To your benefit or your -- I notice that you can't see me now, Mr. President, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the factual description, who can see who. The other was a bit more psychological. Mr. Theunens, Mr. Misetic has some questions for you. If there's any way of moving a tiny little bit, that would ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will also try to move a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think that's better. Hopefully the interpreters in the booth can hear me from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any problem, we will hear from the interpreters or the transcriber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would like to just address one matter, which came up in one of your answers on Tuesday. It is at transcript page 13309, beginning at line 16 and going on to the next page, through line 2. In that line -- or in that paragraph, you say: "However, keeping in mind, I'm sorry, that military discipline is one of the, I will call it, core duties of the operational commander. He is the first one who is responsible, and it's only when there are significant incidents or when the operational commander fails to fulfil his duties that it's only then, that the military police, as well as the military justice system, and military discipline system, of course, I mean, the further steps intervene." And so I'd like to ask you a few questions that are related to this issue. First, I think we've already seen that -- and I won't cover old ground again. I think we have already seen that in the meetings on the 2nd and 3rd of August about providing security in the area. This was done at the level of the MUP and the military police, and General Gotovina was not present nor invited to be present for those meetings. My next question is if you can show me a document that is sent by the MUP to General Gotovina at any time in August or September alerting him or telling him that there is an issue of crime being committed by members of his units in the field. It's a simple -- either there are letters, or there aren't letters. And let me just tell you in advance, I will give you an opportunity at the end to provide any opinion or argument that you wish on what I'm about to do, but if you can just give me factual answers, and then at the end, I will give you an opportunity to provide your opinion. Did you find any such letters from the MUP to General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing such letters from the MUP to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to correspondence from Mr. Lausic to General Gotovina, excluding any documents where the Split Military District or any other Military District is copied on the correspondence, I'm not asking you for documents where Mr. Lausic copies the Split Military District. I'm asking you: Is there any direct correspondence from Mr. Lausic to General Gotovina as the addressee, where Mr. Lausic advises General Gotovina, that he as the operational commander, for example, is failing in his duties which is causing the military police to have to intervene, or something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, excluding the documents that are included in my report, where General Gotovina as well as the other Military District Commanders are copied, I have not seen such a specific letter or complaint from General Lausic to General Gotovina personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to correspondence from members of the international community and organisations, after General Gotovina's meeting with General Forand on the 8th of August, between 8 August and 20 September, is there any correspondence between any international organisation that goes to General Gotovina to advise him of crimes being committed by HV soldiers in his area of responsibility? By crimes, I mean, not -- excluding the issue of the UN vehicles. We're talking about burning, murder, looting, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as to the previous question. I don't remember seeing any complaints by members of the international community or organisations to General Gotovina personally after the 8th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I just would like to make one correction there. There is, of course, the ECMM report, which is not a direct letter of complaint, but the ECMM report which I still have under 65 ter 3419, I believe it has been tendered. It can be found on page 323, part 2, English version. That report suggests that the ECMM monitors who had the meeting with General Gotovina raised the matters of ongoing looting, arson, and harassment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I could go into that with you, but rather than getting into an argument with you, that is why I limited the scope to the 20th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you, obviously, in your report reviewed many presidential transcripts, and in his cross-examination, Mr. Kay pointed out some of the transcripts, where people such as Dr. Radic are telling the president that the civilian authority in Knin is not functioning and, as a result, the burdens, and I'm paraphrasing now, that the burdens on General Cermak are increased as a result of the failures of civilian government. There are other presidential transcripts, some of which are cited in your own report. Did you find a presidential transcript beginning 4 August 1995 all the way to President Tudjman's death in December of 1999, where President Tudjman himself or someone speaking to President Tudjman, mentions General Gotovina failing to take necessary measures regarding the security situation in the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not reviewed all of the presidential transcripts. I reviewed a number of transcripts for 1994 and 1995. Maybe some later ones like the one that covers the meeting between late President Tudjman and General Cermak, but I have not seen in the transcript I have reviewed, which again is not a complete review, any references by President Tudjman or someone speaking to President Tudjman mentioning that General Gotovina failed to take necessary measures regarding the security situation in the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you touched upon a bit the relationship between General Cermak and General Gotovina. You have also mentioned in the cross-examination that General Cermak had meetings with representatives of the international community. Did you find any reports from General Cermak to General Gotovina about his discussions with the members of the international community?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen such reports, and I found that unusual, because I would expect that General Cermak and General Gotovina would have a lot -- I mean, almost daily or at least regular communication, taking into account the specific nature of the situation in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, why would you expect them to have daily communication?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because, first of all, the regulations state that the Military District Commander is responsible for the work of the garrison commander. We have discussed at length that military discipline is -- as, I call it, a core duty of the commander and is of key importance in order to maintain the combat readiness of the armed forces and, in addition, there is the element of the complaints of the international community, and as we have seen, there are several orders to enforce discipline from the various command levels which explicitly refer to the reputation of Croatia which may be endangered by the continuous looting and burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That answer, though, presupposes, does it not that this is the typical situation, for example, you cite in your document the fact that General Gotovina appointed Ashley Minak to be the garrison commander in Benkovac in September. There is a distinction here though with the relationship between General Gotovina and General Cermak, on the one hand, and General Gotovina and the typical garrison commander who is of a much lower rank than a Colonel General, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But again, taking into account the seriousness of the situation, not only in Knin but in the surrounding area, even if the subordination relation between Generals Cermak and Gotovina is, at least based on the material I reviewed, not as cheer as what would one expect in the doctrine, it would still be at least from the military point of view logical that the two of them would meet as often as possible and coordinate their activities and also try to -- to use all the means they have available to them, in order to -- yeah, to solve the situation and end the ongoing crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have -- did you see any evidence, for example, in the Split Military District log-book or any other evidence noting such daily meetings between General Gotovina and General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I did a search in P71, for example, on the name "Cermak" or "garrison commander," and I believe there was only one reference at somewhere very far to the end, which, again, I consider unusual. I remember seeing General Cermak on the video you showed which allegedly depicts or transmits the -- a meeting held on the 5th or the 6th of August. Otherwise, no references to General Cermak in P71.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's close this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could call up Exhibit D818 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: While I'm bringing it up. This is a request. You cited it in your report. It's a request from General Gotovina to General Cermak. Now, I understand that there are some documents titled "Order," but I believe most of those documents that go to the garrison in Knin are also copied to other garrisons, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But in their personal dealings, between the two men, I'm pulling up this exhibit, because when General Gotovina has to address General Cermak personally, is it typical -- or isn't it unusual if, in fact, there's a superior/subordinate relationship that the superior commander sends a request and gives his military greetings at the end as opposed to issuing an order, and then the typical last sentence would say: I hereby make ... in this case it would say, I hereby make Ivan Cermak for executing this order. Wouldn't that be the typical formulation that General Gotovina would usu when addressing a subordinate, based on your review of all of documents of the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And actually I would see less of a problem in the use of the word "request." Again, when looking at the word "request" in the context of the contents of the document, but I was -- I found the use of -- when you look at the first sentence, in future please do not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you, because I found that too, and there may be in an additional translation issue there. Because in the Croatian it actually says [B/C/S spoken], which is not quite the same way -- it doesn't give the same sense in the English. You have raised the issue now. I wasn't going to raise it with the translation service. I am fully aware that it is improper to ask the interpreters to do this, Mr. President, but I will leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three words only, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Four words. [B/C/S spoken] [Interpretation] General, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, sir, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the words are put to you, but I heard them being spoken by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, although against the rules, I appreciate the assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you have reviewed General Gotovina documents. When he is addressing the OG commanders; when he is addressing other garrison commanders, he doesn't say, Sir, please, right? He doesn't have to say please to anyone that is it subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He doesn't address them as sir. That's not typical in any military, is it, that a superior addresses a subordinate as sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in some armies people love to use the word, sir, but I mean, it is not a usual practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you'll call from our meeting in January that I raised the issue with you based on your experience in the Belgian army. The situation here is that General Gotovina and General Cermak both were of the same rank at that time, Colonel Generals, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us a little bit from a military perspective, is it usual to put two soldiers of the same rank at the level of Colonel Generals and have one in command of the other?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can happen. And then in case there is a problem that may arise, I mean, the situation should be clear from the position they hold because one position should be higher or superior to the other one. Now, if you have two people with the same rank in a position at the same level but still a requirement for one having authority over the other in my army, but I don't know exactly for the Croatian army, the seniority in the rank, i.e., how many years does that person have that rank will determine then who has authority over whom. But that is a very specific case where have you two people with the same rank holding the same position. For example, two Brigadier commanders who are part of the same corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to say one had authority over the other. But I would agree with you that there is an -- in the collegiality between officers of the same rank -- I'm not talking about command here. I'm just saying in terms of the respect between the two, the person who has held the rank longer enjoys a certain level of deference or respect because he has held the rank longer, in military culture I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but, I mean, the rank is a starting point. And if they have the same rank, then you lock at the position. As I said well, one position should be superior to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. Sorry to interrupt you, but I agree with you. That is how, typically, you would look at things. But I think you in your own report say the situation is not clear. So what I'm trying to do is in this type of situation where it is it not clear.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay, then what I'm saying is let's look to other factors. And one of the things that I'd like you to tell us is in military culture, would you agree that the -- if there are two persons of equal rank in terms of the culture not in terms of now, you know, command issues, but just in terms of culture. The culture is the person who has held the rank longer enjoys a certain deference, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and even if he's at a higher age just as a matter of courtesy, without having any operational implications, the person with a higher age may be addressed in a more -- probably be addressed in a more respectful manner but the person in the younger age, even if they have the same rank and hold a position which is at the same level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So as between these two men who held the rank longer of Colonel General?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Ivan Cermak was promoted to General -- Colonel General at an early stage, but it was a reserve rank, but I have not seen any distinction being made between reserve and active duty ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, are you aware of the fact that General Gotovina was only promoted to the rank of Colonel General a few days before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, and I have referred to that in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So does the fact -- does this indicate to you why the relationship between the two men wasn't as clear as you would expect typically a Military District Commander and a garrison commander, the typical relationship that they would have?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obviously one of the aspects that should be taken into account when one tries to establish the relationship between the two. Another aspect as I addressed earlier would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Someone creates some noise. And is invited not to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, another very important aspect would be the communication between the two of them to see what is the nature of the communication, do we see orders being issued from one to the other, reports being provided by one to the other, other documents, what kind of wording is used in these documents.
