Now, I must say what I really missed was, in addition to reports of -- of communications between the General Gotovina and Cermak, was also an order specifying the duties of General Cermak, because, as I have tried to show in the report, based on his activities, I came to the conclusion that his duties were much further ranging than the duties one would expect from a, call it, traditional garrison commander as it is stipulated in the doctrine. And obviously the duties -- the fact that General Cermak was exercising much wider duties and powers than a traditional garrison commander should also be taken into account, when analysing the relationship between General Cermak and General Gotovina. I have an entry in the report where General Cermak states -- this is 65 ter 751. This is a report to the HV Main Staff dated 25th August. General Cermak states that the Split Military District Command and the Knin garrison command are constant coordination. Again when we compare that with the doctrine, that is a -- unusual description because a garrison commander should, at least according to doctrine, be subordinated to the district commander, and coordination does not necessarily imply subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My concern is basically with the issue of reporting, and so let me sum this up. There are no letters written by MUP to General Gotovina in this time-period, no letters written --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think these questions have been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I know. It's leading to a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leading to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me give you the background and then pose the question to you. You agree with me that MUP doesn't write any letters to General Gotovina in August and September, that General Lausic doesn't write any letters to General Gotovina personally in August or September, the international representatives of organisations don't write to General Gotovina certainly between 8 August and 20 September, 1995. You agree me that you haven't seen any reports from General Cermak on his meetings with the international representatives that go to General Gotovina. I think we covered the last time I questioned you the fact that this meeting in Plitvice on the 15th of September is between the MUP and the military police with no representatives of the Split Military District present. My question to you is: Based on all of those facts, isn't it logical to conclude that if, in fact, you were right that all of these people had to act only because the operational commander "failed to fulfil his duties," that somebody over this six-week to two-month period would have thought it appropriate to make write General Gotovina a letter?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first like to clarify your interpretation of my answer. That is that my answer is based on the documents I have reviewed. I do not know what is put in documents I have not seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, we're not interested -- we're only interested in what you know based on what you reviewed, and obviously we could always in any case say there might be something out there that we don't know. Let's talk about what we do know.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, but just for the accuracy, I wanted to mention that now. I think the fundamental problem is that a military commander does not have to wait for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's not my question, Mr. Theunens. I'm just asking you based on common sense and your knowledge of this -- the military and how things work, isn't it extremely unlikely that if you were right that all of these people had to act only because the operational commander failed to fulfil his duties, isn't it extremely unlikely that no one would have thought to write General Gotovina a letter in this time-period and say, Hey, we're having a problem because you're failing to do your job? Isn't it extremely unlikely that someone wouldn't have gone to the president and said, We're having all these problems because the operational commander is failing to fulfil his duties. You agree with me that that is extremely unlikely?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you take the answer I gave to a question, I think, it was by Mr. Kay. You take that answer out of context because I provided a similar but more comprehensive reply to a similar question you asked me while you were cross-examining me. The doctrine is very clear on the duties of the commander, the commander has to maintain discipline. He must keep abreast with the situation in his units, he must consider all aspects of the situation and assess it rapidly, i.e., it is husband duty to maintain discipline in thinks units, and this is done through the chain of command. During one of the breaks, I made a list of orders General Gotovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we've covered this ground --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you are entering another area, what should be done, and what should be -- what should trigger any activity, et cetera. Mr. Misetic is asking you, apparently, an assessment, he asks you whether it would be logical to assume that someone would have stood up and would is have said, General Gotovina, what's happening here? Nothing ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But when we look again at P71, for example, so the operational diary, and the things being said at the meetings, the daily command meetings, during operation Ljeto, for example, as well as during Operation Storm, the people present are indeed complaining about crimes committed, there is looting, there is burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this is all stuff that you're now going back to what is being discussed internally in the Split Military District. And, of course, every segment of the Croatian system has a certain role to play. But the issue is, you said that these other organs, the military police, the military justice system, et cetera, it's only when the operational commander fails to fulfil his duties that they have to intervene. So let's take it out of the context of what's being discussed internally within the Split Military District, and I'm putting it to you that if, in fact, these other organs of the Croatian system, the military police, the military disciplinary system, and others, the civilian police, the civilian system, the international organisations on the ground, and references in the presidential transcripts, let me just put it to you, if, in fact, all of these people had to act because as you say the operational commander was failing to fulfil his duties, isn't it logical to conclude that someone, anyone, in those organisations, would have alerted General Gotovina to the problem, if, in fact, they were having to act only because he was failing to fulfil his duties?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, but I wouldn't expect, for example, the civilian police to do so. We see the civilian police complains to the military police, and that the military police administration issues orders via the professional chain to the military police battalions, as well as the document you asked me it exclude where General Lausic makes certain suggestions in order to improve the situation which is sent for info to the Military District Commanders. More importantly, I would like to address -- to draw your attention to the orders issued by General Cervenko who is the best placed individual in this system of command and control because he is the chief of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm going stop you. You what you are doing, is you are explaining how it all should have functioned. Now -- and what actually happened. Now, Mr. Misetic is putting, however, a different question to you. The question being that if due to the failure to take action, the various units, but they're not in a military sense, but the various bodies would have to act on their own behave would it be logical to expect that one of these bodies would have said, Why do we not get instructions? Why do we have to act on our own? Why is there no effective command in this respect, to the extent that there was subordination? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I understand the question. We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then try to -- for you, perhaps start answering another question. The issue is if General Gotovina did not take the proper action and that he left it to all the others to figure out by themselves what to do and what not to do, would it be logical to expect that one of these elements, whatever you call it, would have sent him a letter or given him a phone call, or address him and say, Why do we have to figure out for ourselves? Why don't you take the lead? That's Mr. Misetic, how I understood your question more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am confused, because I tried to answer the question based on my military background. And I -- I mean, the most logical would be that the superior of General Gotovina, i.e., the chief of the Main Staff, speaks to him and says, Look, I have receiving these reports from the military police, and it's not going well. What are you doing? What's happening? I have so say, I have not seen such instructions or reports or -- or other forms of communication by General Cervenko to General Gotovina specifically. What I have seen and that is included in the report are orders by General Gotovina -- excuse me, General Cervenko to the Military District Commanders to enforce discipline to take all necessary measures and so on and so on, and we see that these orders are being forwarded through the chain of command. Again, from a military point of view, it would be unusual for the civilian police to address General Gotovina directly. What we have is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Misetic focussed his question on internal military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we know that General Forand wrote him a letter on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think you know, Mr. Theunens, that I said between 8 August and 20 September after General Forand finally got a chance to meet General Gotovina on the 8th, right, he never writes him another letter asking him to intervene on issues of crimes, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say it's something have you to address with General Forand. I cannot explain why he didn't do that. He must have will his reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you one final point -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I wanted to say, like, it is rather unusual for an army that, unless you have really serious problems, that you expect the representatives of the international community to assist you in -- in actually notifying the commander that there is a problem in that army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not saying they were asking them to assist him. Although obviously if the international community representatives or persons on the ground see crimes, they should report it. But what I'm telling you is, there, in fact, was reporting being done and meetings being held at various levels between the international agencies and organs of the Croatian government. Those weren't taking place concerning crime between General Gotovina and those agencies -- and those international agencies, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But again, we don't know whether General Gotovina was meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What we don't know, we don't know, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, exactly. If there is it no meeting whatsoever between General Gotovina and these representatives of the internation community, it is quite obvious that they cannot raise the issue of lack of discipline or crimes with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I think that the question included the possibility, did you ask for a meeting for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I have not systemically reviewed requests by representatives of the international community, be it UNCRO, ECMM, ICRC, other organisations in the area for meetings with General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you have raised the issue of General Cervenko. Let me say this: General Cervenko on specific issues that he has with General Gotovina, you have put in your report, that he did send very specific orders to General Gotovina to report to him, one being this alleged threat to Alun Roberts, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And demanded that General Gotovina explain the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How does that arise out of the original comment? This all much of it could have been raised in the original cross-examination in -- between General Cermak and General Gotovina, and we are, by the way, far beyond 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. President, the issue is I only raised it because, I believe, the witness now in his answer said -- mentioned General Cervenko as being one of the persons who would address with them, but if that's not in dispute with the Prosecution, that's fine with me. I'm just trying to point out that General Cervenko did raise specific issues that he had with General Gotovina, one of them being this alleged threat to Alun Roberts which is in evidence now. And I was going ask Mr. Theunens if there is an similar warning or report or order from General Cervenko to General Gotovina saying, I hear that you are failing in your duties to maintain discipline. Please report to me as to why this is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documents I have reviewed, I have not seen a specific warning from General Cervenko to General Gotovina except for the Roberts' one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Theunens, I thank you very much for your time. You have been with us for so long that I'm already nostalgic, and you haven't left yet, but thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The feeling is mutual, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, Judge Gwaunza has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Theunens, during cross-examination, you were shown some documents that you stated you had not seen before, and I think you even said some of them were important and that had you seen them, you would have made reference to them or used them in your analysis. My question is: Do you think that the information contained in those documents might have affected some of your conclusions, and, if so, to what extent? And perhaps it's a general question, but perhaps in your response you can be more specific in your answers, if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. It is correct that there are documents which I would like to have included even if it was just to be more complete in the report. However, I do not remember that have I been shown any documents during cross-examination which would lead me to review any of, what I would call, significant conclusions drawn in the report. It is obvious, for example, that I would have included a conclusion on, for example, the documents Mr. Kay showed, that the military police reports discussing or mentioning crimes and incidents in the zone of responsibility of the Knin garrison, that they were not sent to General Cermak. This would certainly be something I would have included because I consider it significant, even though in the context of General Cermak, in my view, it does not affect the conclusion I drew that he was the most senior military/civilian authority in Knin. Because I drew that conclusion based on the activities of General Cermak. But it would have been useful, as I said, to have these documents and then to add a sentence in relation to the enforcement of military discipline; however, General Cermak was not receiving reports compiled by the military police, even though they were sent to his counterpart in the Split garrison. Than is the main example I remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I have got a question for you as well. And for the parties. It is relates to page 13234 at the end. You were asked about Mr. Zidovec who is asking for the submission of information from the police administration, because they're necessary for compiling reports. He wants information about the clearing up of bodies. The question was whether if Mr. Cermak was part of the operation for dealing with this matter, whether he would not have been requested to provide this information as well. Now, in your answer, you said -- you said: "Not from the military point of view." And then I think it was Mr. Kay continued by saying: "We're not looking at a military document. We're looking at the -- at a Ministry of Interior document." My question to you is the following: Is it usual if military and civilian organisations, units, are participating in the same operation, coordinated operation, cooperation between the various segments, is it usual that the -- well, let's say, the civilian authorities would include the military counterpart taking part in such an operation to report to them on the matter as well? So it's like cross-reporting from one system, military system, to the other system, the civilian system, although working together and being involved in -- in joint operations, perhaps even under the command of one or at least -- where the one authority takes the lead and is in charge of the operation, is it usual that you then would seek across the division lines information for the purposes of reporting within your own structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there are several aspects, Your Honour, or several aspects. The military component and the civilian component will report for sure through their own chains. However -- and it will depend on the nature of the cooperation or the situation we're looking at, there must be a system whereby they can exchange the information. And one would also except there would be a consolidated report then, whereby the information that is reported through the military chain which is considered relevant for the civilians and vice versa is exchanged and available to all. But such a consolidated report will include information that is included also in the separate reports, but the information that is included in the separate reports, all of it does not necessarily have to be included in the consolidated report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who would ask for the consolidated report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend of who is in charge and what has been agreed. And it depends -- I mean, the civilians and the military are conducting a particular activity. Somebody or a body must have given instructions for that activity and that body should then also be informed about the level of implementation of the activity, i.e., to see whether the instructions it has given are being implemented, and a consolidated report that -- that includes both civilian and military information would be an appropriate manner to ensure this information of the body that has issued the task, or that is in charge of the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kay did apparently put some weight on Mr. Cermak not being included in the persons or organs asked for information. Would you, from your experience, would you give a similar significance to Mr. Cermak not being included in those who were asked to report, in view of -- as an indicator for the role he played in the operation of clearing up bodies?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I -- I stated that I was not aware of the existence or the activities of civilian defence clearing teams, which could well have operated outside the authority of General Cermak. The information I included in my report on the clearing of bodies was based on the reports provided by the Brigadier there, I don't remember his exact name, but Biskovic, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Brkic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brkic, thank you. And did he not explicitly mention the activities of civilian teams. It is logical that the civilian defence teams will send reports on their activities to -- through their civilian chain, the MUP chain. It is also logical that if General Cermak was in charge of the overall clearing of bodies that he should have been informed, one way or the other, of the activities of the civilian teams, and I don't remember seeing documents, specific documents, sent by these civilian defence teams to General Cermak. So the fact that the civilian defence teams sent reports through the civilian chain - I think those were the reports Mr. Kay show - does not allow to conclude or to draw conclusions whether or not they share this information or similar information with Mr. Cermak, or General Cermak. Because what I have seen again, based on the documents, these report chains are kept separate, even though there may be consolidated reports whereby a document is sent -- is addressed to both chains to both the military as well as the civilian. It's -- I mean, we're three-weeks into this exercise, but I don't remember a specific civilian document being also addressed -- I mean, not only through the civilian chain but also to the military addressees, except for military police reporting where we are talking about the orders -- and, no, and even there I believe it is still different or separate because, for example, when Mr. Moric complained to General Lausic about the ineffectiveness of the military police, and we see then that the General Lausic may forward the letter of Mr. Moric or takes out the relevant components for the military police in a specific document he compiled or the military police compiled themselves which is addressed to the military police units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You mentioned civilian Defence, you mean civilian protection, don't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I have a correction, rather than a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That being clarified. This means that this concludes your rather lengthy testimony in this court. Mr. Theunens, usually I would excuse you at this moment, but perhaps we have to deal with quite a number of documents. And exceptionally I would ask to you stay with us when we're dealing with that. It might be that we need your help at any given moment, so if you would be so kind to stay for another, perhaps, ten minutes. Because I would like to deal with -- especially the bar table documents at this moment. We have -- let's start with the Cermak bar table lists. We have six submissions, Mr. Waespi. The first one, on the task and job of the Knin garrison; second, passage of journalists at -- and other matters; various topics, and I gave the date, the 4th of December; the 5th is the daily reports of the 72nd Battalion. That's number 5 of the 9th of December 2008; and, finally, the 6th one, criminal reports filed by the 72nd Battalion of the military police directly to the military prosecutor, also the 9th of December. Now, I think we know that there are no objections against the first and the third, which means that we have not heard the position of the Prosecution on the second bar table submission, passage of journalists and other matters, 3rd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We have no objections to the second one either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. The fourth, military police rotation of Knin Independent Company members and other orders and reports by the Knin company, 5th December 2008. Any objections against those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think I responded last night to the Defence. I don't think there are objections to the fourth bar table motions either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did object, or you did --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was agreed last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was agreed. That's -- Then we move to the fifth, daily reports, 72nd Battalion, 9th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's the stipulation part. We don't have an objection to -- as we said, to it coming in as a stipulation, that all these documents refer to the same issue and were sent to these ten addressees, and the Knin garrison isn't part it. That's -- we can agree on the stipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stipulation is the character of the documents, and the documents as such are admissible. Do I understand? Or would we refrain from admission at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The issue is just if we stipulate to that, you know, the documents don't need to come in. If the documents come in as well, we need translations according to standard practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then if you have stipulations on the matter, Of course, the Chamber would like to have it -- even if one -- if only in one or two lines to have this stipulation clearly on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've drafted the stipulation in uncontroversial terms. We have listed the documents because those documents will be committed to translation, there will be Defence experts referring to them, if we get to that stage, and so they are material. We understand the problems of the translation department. It's going to take many weeks for them to deal with that, than is a way of dealing with the issue now in a satisfactory way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there is no urgency at this moment in the translation, the stipulation, and the list of documents can be put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said uncontroversially you have formulated the stipulation. How to have this on the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think during the next break, we'll just figure out these one or two sentences. I see them before me, but perhaps we can just finalize them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the Chamber, then, at this moment expects you to do is to read the exact formulation of the stipulation into the record and to make a joint filing of the list, not the documents, the list of documents that stipulation relates to. If that would be filed, then we have, for the time being, a complete record, and, Mr. Kay, further translations and how to use these documents in any further stages of these proceedings when it comes to that. We'll wait and see, but we have resolved the issue as it stands now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. So five receives a special treatment. The sixth category, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We have reviewed it last night. We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then, Mr. Registrar, you are invited on the basis of the first, the second, the third, the fourth, and the sixth bar table submissions to assign exhibit numbers to them. No exhibit numbers will yet be assigned to the documents listed and to be filed as we find it in the fifth submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure you have addressed the third one, and maybe it's been dealt with. We added a few comments in a separate Prosecution comment section, and I think that should be fine as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's been included, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I received the Cermak Defence report saying additionally the Defence and the Prosecution agreed on contents and comments of the third bar table submission. That is the description. It's not about admissibility. It is about how they are described and how they will find their way in the list of exhibits. May I take it, Mr. Kay, that the agreement is reflected in the list as sent to Mr. Registrar to assign numbers to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely. There have been several exchanges on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Registrar, who will have to finally assign numbers to these documents, is provided with the final formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Number 5 which still has to be formulated into a filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about 3, because that was the third submission which Mr. Waespi raised. Then the registrar, and I repeat that, is invited to the assign numbers to the exhibits we find in the first, second, third, fourth, and sixth bar table submissions. And the Chamber will then, once numbers have been assigned, decide on admission. These were the Defence bar table submissions. I suggest that we first go to the Prosecution bar table submissions - let me find it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure that we have submitted it to -- to Your Honours. We did to the Defence last night. This is a fairly different to, you know, the 200 or so exhibits we wanted to have admitted, you know, four, five weeks ago. What we have at this point in time are two separate submissions, one is a normal bar table motion. I think it is 12 documents that are referenced in Mr. Theunens's report. Not discussed in court. We would like to have these admitted, and I can -- as soon as we have time shortly, can submit it to you. And the second document is a list of, I think, 29 documents. These are all the documents that have been referred to by Mr. Theunens in the course of his examination but have not been entered, and a couple were added today. So we will submit this list. We did already to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll prepare lists for that so that we can deal with those lists in a similar way as we dealt with the bar table submissions, Although they are not really bar table submissions because the list of 29 are documents that were dealt with during the testimony of Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is correct. The first one is more akin to a normal bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll deal with them. Then we have a few other documents which were MFIed and are not part of lists. The first one would be D01079. I think, Mr. Mikulicic, it was you who tendered this document. Yes. The issue for the Chamber was that you presented it, Mr. Mikulicic, as more or less a -- it was a document dated the 30th of December, 2005, a document -- a letter sent by the Ministry of Justice of Croatia to Miroslav Separovic. And you introduced it, it's a formal document. It states to some extent, the legislation, laws as applicable. I think on that basis, you sought admission. Mr. Waespi did not object, but the Chamber said we'd like to have a closer look at this document. Looking at this document, apart from reflecting what we also heard during the testimony, that is, how the structure was of the various judicial or semi-judicial organs and who was appointed at what time, recruited from where, et cetera, it also contains a factual section, and I ask you to read with me the very end of this document, where it says: "In conclusion, in the period your letter is regarding to, and pursuant to the ZOUP decrees in force at the time, MUP disciplinary courts were established, which conducted disciplinary proceedings, in cases of disciplinary violations committed by the MUP officials on duty, or regarding their duty. In their proceedings a high number of various types of penalties were dispensed." This is a statement, not of the law, but of facts; that is, how they functioned. What the high number exactly would come down to, the various types of penalties in relation to what kind of violations of discipline, that's all rather factual. Of course, the Chamber would have to digest that. And to give it any sense, of course, you would want to know what the various types of penalties would be and what a high number would be, well, Mr. Waespi has not objected to it. At the same time, the Chamber is, of course, concerned how to deal with it. I mean, how to introduce this in the evaluation of the totality of the evidence. It's not primarily the legal matters, what decrees were there, who was -- because we heard about that a bit in the testimony as well. But it's especially the -- this portion which I read to you, which bothers us a bit, and if it does not bother Mr. Waespi, then, of course, we would have to consider how to proceed, but I just put to you so that we can finally decide on admission, or if you say, That is not really the part which is of importance for us. It was mainly the legal part and how the structure was, then there might even be a possibility to come to a commonly redacted the document. But the factual part is without any -- at this moment without sufficient support, factual support.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. A point I made yesterday, I would like to receive that initial request from the Defence. I think it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another matter that was on the record, and Mr. Mikulicic agreed that he would give that to you. Has this been done already, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour this has been done in the way that we enter it, the request for the Defence into the system, and we're asking for the translation of the initial document, upon which was issued the documents from the ministry. On the other side, I can see clearly your point, Your Honour, and I would like to stress is that the only concern of the Defence as its regards to this document is a legal matter, so we are not paying much attention on the very bottom of the documents that have you just read. So, if it is possible to have this document entered into evidence under these circumstances, it is okay with the Defence. We will not be asking more of it. On the other side, we could explore the fact portions, so-called, in the documents with another witness in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I just would like to have a look at the translated request, and then we can come to you with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it for the time being to the parties for whether the appropriate action to take would be, for example, to take out the last three lines that deals with facts and have a -- have a redacted version tendered into evidence and admitted into evidence or whether the parties agree that at this moment no factual support for rather blunt factual statements are there, so that the parties agree that the Chamber, on the basis of this alone, could ignore this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that could be of any assistance, we are prepared to withdraw the request for entering this document into the evidence until we would have a final translation of the Defence request for the documents, plus the tables that are attached to these documents that concerns to the sanctions that has been put upon the violation of the disciplinary. So maybe it will be the most practical solution that in this very moment, we will withdraw request for tendering this documents, and we will put it in front of the witness which we -- who we estimate it as a proper one in a due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think as a practical matter, it is probably safer to keep it as MFIed because it has been referred to in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mikulicic, if you say the tables attached to this document. I, however, see that it is uploaded now as a two-page document without any tables, so the reference to the tables in relation to D1079 is unclear it me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, maybe I wasn't clear enough. The last reference in the documents is referring to the tables which are originally attached to this document, and these tables we have in our documentary evidence, prepared for Defence. So we didn't ask for tendering those tables in a time when I was requesting to tender two pages document into the evidence, but we believe that the whole document could be show up to the proper witness in the due course, together with the attached tables, which are basically referring to the last portion of the documents that you have just been reading aloud in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I note that no reference is made in this part of the letter to any attachment. Therefore, I leave it up to you. We keep it MFIed, and we further discuss, perhaps including the attachments with Mr. Waespi. You see how it could be introduced. For the time being it's clear to the Chamber that you're seeking to introduce the information of a primarily legal character and not about how --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. And I think is a more practical solution just to solve the problem in a conversation with Mr. Waespi, and I'm sure we could solve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber waits for a report on that. Then we have D01083 is still pending for translation. Finally, we have the expert report by Mr. Theunens, P1113. We have the addendum to the report, P1114. And we have the corrigenda to the expert report, P115. The Chamber at the time said that it would decide on admission once we would have heard the testimony of Mr. Theunens. Are there any submissions to be made in addition to the many submissions already made in respect of the admissibility of the report, its addendum, and the corrigendum? No need. Then the Chamber will decide on admission. Finally, I still have to find out further about P1118. Can't deal with at this moment. Then we have P1138. That is the Lausic report concerning inspection. It's a document dated -- it's about an inspection between the 17th and the 20th of October, 1995. When it was tendered, I think it was you, Mr. Misetic, you said, Well, we'll introduce the document or the full -- the broader, entire document. That's what you said you do. Have we seen this document in that other broader?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have. There is an technical issue, and I -- I let the Chamber decide how to deal with it. I don't have the number in front of me right now, and I trust that my case manager will assist me. We introduced a document which was the overall inspection conducted by the Main Staff of the Split -- inspection of the Split Military District. I think that report is dated 30 October -- I'm sorry, it's the 25th of October, 1995 -- actually, no. One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll find the date, Your Honour, but there is an inspection. I believe, it is the 30th of October. This report is an attachment to that inspection. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it ever comes to that, the Appeals Chamber might struggle with it or the Chamber when preparing the determinations we'll have to make.
