utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would -- uploaded again. But now including the document which was MFIed as P1138.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then P1138 would be vacated. Is that -- Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That being resolved, is there any other matter in relation to the exhibits as far as we can deal with them now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record, what we were discussing is Exhibit D987, and the Defence will then take -- sorry. Exhibit P1138 MFI, and we'll upload it so that it is appended to Exhibit D987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is now clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, often we had to ask your assistance. Now we asked to you wait, and we didn't further rely on you. Nevertheless, thank you for that. Usually I thank witnesses and experts for coming a long way to The Hague. I will refrain from that. But this does not in any way affect our thanks for your coming and having answered many, many, many questions of the parties and of the Bench. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wonder whether it would be a good idea to deal with a matter in relation to the next witness before the break. There was a -- let me just find it. Yes. There was a Prosecution motion to add 11 documents to the 65 ter list to be used with Witness 90. The -- I think two Defence teams -- I think it was Gotovina Defence and the Cermak Defence did not object to adding to them, but we received this morning a courtesy copy of a response to be filed by the Markac Defence, which objects against admission of these documents to the 65 ter list. Does this trigger -- of course, the Chamber will have to decide. We have received the submissions. Is there anything else we would have to deal with? If not, we most likely will decide the matter during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess from our standpoint, it sort of also dovetails into the potential bar table submission matter that is going to be made relating to this witness, again, using many of the documents or some of the documents that are going to be proposed to added to the 65 ter list. I don't know if the Court wants to hear any argument on the matter or not. We have put our objections down with respect to the specific -- the real issue is relevance. It's really not necessarily that the -- putting it on the list at this late stage is a problem, but the real issue is the relevance of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which, of course, affects both adding them to the 65 ter list and at later stage admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think our submission really expresses our specific objections to the relevance of the documents, and it will go along way to expressing our submission on the bar table submission for some, if not all of the documents that were included on this list and others. So I guess I will not add anything more than what I have said and what's in our written submission are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just in response to the courtesy copy of the motion I received this morning, just point out at paragraph 2, the Defence says that - the Defence for Mr. Markac - says that it does not oppose the addition of the 11 documents to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list, and that is the only application the Prosecution has made with the motion to add. So if we take it with the two-step process, if the Defence for Mr. Markac does not oppose the addition of the documents to the 65 ter list, then I believe there is no objection for the motion to add before Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I then take it -- that's how I understood the observation just made is that even if you add them to the 65 ter list, it says passe, then it opposes very much the arguments used and that this will have an effect on admission which is the next step. I mean, to be on the 65 ter list as such, doesn't hurt, if I could say so. If it is mainly on the basis of relevance. Of course, relevance is also an important aspect of admission because, as we all know, it's relevance and probative value that are the key elements for a decision to admit evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have anything much to add to the motion where we have demonstrated clearly relevance and probative value, but if, of course, in the motion we do not go into detail, but if we go through the testimony of this witness, the additional relevance and the additional probative value will be clear to the Chambers. But I believe we have clearly demonstrated relevance and probative value in the motion to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is a backward approach to say we'll demonstrate how they're relevant when the witness testifies. They need to be demonstrated now before witness comes on the stand. Because to say that they are relevant without any real explanation for why they're relevant without having the witness testify is the wrong way to go with it. Tell us the specific reasons why they're relevant for the proposition they stand for in their 65 ter motion to add them to their list, other than saying that they're relevant. Just saying that they're relevant means nothing. The specific reasons for why they're relevant is what we need to know. Because they're not stated, and I won't go any further, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We have stated very clearly why they're relevant. If it is necessary, I could do it even in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter and decide. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is an Latin saying litis finire oportet, which means at a certain we have to stop argument, and there should be an end to that. Nevertheless, the Chamber decided to grant two minutes, and I will look at the clock, two minutes this time is 120 seconds to further deal with the matter of the artillery documents, and the primary reason why the Chamber grants a request to make further submissions on it is that the Chamber, first of all, would like to know how disclosure actually took place. Whether it is appropriate or inappropriate the way it was done, but we, of course, uploading in e-court is one thing, releasing documents, not everything that's uploaded in e-court is available to everyone. That may be of some relevance. So we would like to know what actually happened, if the parties are agreement on that. It could be that just one of the parties says what is done. Perhaps, Mr. Russo, you would be the most appropriate person to do that. And if that's not challenged, then we do not have to spend time on that. Therefore, it's -- Mr. Russo, you have 120 seconds starts in two seconds from now. They have started.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me say first that disclosure was made, we believe, on 20th May this year. However, we were unable to confirm what was actually contained on the CD that was disclosed on the 20th of May. Out of an over abundance of caution, we re-disclosed the documents via e-mail on 9th December, and then uploaded into e-court. So the disclosure was made at the very latest on the 9th December, via e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's 40 seconds. Mr. Misetic, your 120 seconds start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we filed our response on the 2nd of December so that would mean at the time we filed our response, it was before this most recent disclosure. The second issue is I'm not sure I understand Mr. Russo's position because based on their position at footnote 7 of their reply which was filed yesterday, it says that the translations of the eight documents referred to in footnote 13 of the response were uploaded into e-court in May 2008.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And have been re-disclosed to the Defence. So I don't know -- if I understood Mr. Russo correctly, he is now saying that he believes there was a that CD disclosed, but they can't show it. The reply says that it was disclosed by uploading into e-court which is why we had asked for a very sort amount of time to so reply, which is that our position is that uploading documents into e-court is not proper disclose under the rules. That should be done under Rule 66 and 68, and the Defence does not have an obligation to constantly monitor e-court to see if there's something new in there and then to approach Prosecution to see if they intend to disclose this, use it, et cetera. So that's our position, Your Honour, and if I'm mistaken on this, I will certainly work with the Prosecution to see how this disclosure was done in May. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it that the inappropriateness -- the Chamber just looked at your submission in which you are seeking leave to -- to make further submissions, and that's then part of what we've heard now in the 240 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even less, but 240 seconds reserved for you. Mr. Russo, you reserved 40 seconds, I don't think you want to add anything, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour, other than to request leave to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The remaining seconds certainly will assist interpreters and transcribers to take a breath. This -- the Chamber will, of course, decide the matter. Mr. Russo, or do I have to address you for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Yes, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not visible for me at the moment. First of all, the Chamber has considered the objections against adding the 11 documents to the 65 ter list, where I would say 95 per cent of argument was relevance, and only a small portion of the -- of the objection made by the Markac Defence, only, was the fair trial issue as we find it in paragraph 18 of the response. The Chamber denies the objection. If the late adding to the 65 ter list would cause considerable problems in preparing for the examination of this witness, or if investigation -- further investigations would be needed, of course, the Chamber expects the Markac Defence to address the Chamber on that specific issue. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to call your next witness? No protective measures, if I'm well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact, we have not had any communication this witness at all. Therefore, I do not know, and in an abundance of caution, perhaps he could be brought it in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then we have to go into closed session, which means curtains down, although there is a fair chance that they will be back up again in two or three minutes. We turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Turkalj, you'll first be examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to examine Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could be please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name is Josip Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Currently I am employed in the Ministry of the Interior in the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During 1995, what was your position within the special police sector?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, I was at the post of the commander of the anti-terrorist unit, Lucko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On 3rd and 4th February, 2004, were you interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the course of that interview when questions were asked from you, did you respond truthfully?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, as far as I was able to remember facts and details, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At that time, did you provide a signed statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed a statement that was read back to me from the English language.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it read back to you in the Croatian language to you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was read out to me in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: After that, on 11th March, 2005, were you interviewed again by members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Another interview was conducted with me. I'm not sure about the date, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And on that occasion, when you were asked questions, did you respond truthfully?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to tell the truth at all times, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was that interview video-recorded?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was video-recorded, but I did not view the recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document number 6160, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, were you provided with copies of your statement of 3rd and 4th February, 2004, and the transcripts of your interview of 2005, about a few weeks back by the Croatian authorities with a request to review them in anticipation of your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statements were sent to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you examine your statement made in 2004? Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I reviewed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did the contents of that statement accurately reflect what you stated to the investigators and the members of the Office of the Prosecutor on 3rd and 4th February, 2004?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially the contents are correct, though I would have certain corrections to make in relation to four portions of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And can you -- we will bring up that statement on the screen, Mr. Turkalj, and would you please then identify to us what these corrections are. Do you see the document on the screen? That the statement you made in 2004? If you could perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, if we could provide a hard copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask him. I take it that if he has identified four portions which are in need of correction. Did you bring your own copy where you made have made notes as to what to correct, Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have my copy of the statement with me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a hard copy, if that could be provided to Mr. Turkalj. It is easier than to read from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The binder also has a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, the statement is right at the top, under the tab number 1. And could you please tell Court -- refer to the paragraph numbers and tell us what the correction is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to make a correction in paragraph 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And can you tell what the correction is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to correct the last sentence, where I said that we were at a meeting in Knin, since this was not a formal meeting but an informal conversation in relation to certain events where information was exchanged on the life and circumstances in Knin prevailing at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it meet your concern if we would make it: I left the room whilst the other persons present continued their conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be correct, had I left the room ahead of the others. But I noticed since I spent some five minutes lingering in the corridor, that the others followed suit soon after me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not part of your testimony you give at this moment. So we then change: I left the room whilst the other persons present continued their conversation. And we take out: The meeting was still going on. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You indicated, Mr. Turkalj, that you had four. What are the other three corrections?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the statement and would like to correct a statement under paragraph 61.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Go ahead, and let us know what the correction is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part of statement, I highlighted the fact that with my associates, I asked from General Markac that Mr. Drljo be thrown out of the Lucko Unit, which was, I believe, translated differently. We had informal conversations when we would happen upon General Cermak that Mr. Drljo should be transferred to a different post within the sector of the special police. The reason behind that request was the fact that Mr. Drljo did not fully respect the authority of the superior. It was difficult to work with him because of that fact, and because of these minor difficulties, we believed it better for him to be transferred to a new post, to a different post.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Can we just have clarification on the last paragraph there, because General Cermak's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That what I was on about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, you referred to General Cermak, or I think it has been noted as General Cermak. Did you mean to say General Cermak, or did you mean to say General Markac? Let me read back to you what you have said. You said: "We had informal conversations when we would happen upon General Cermak, that Mr. Drljo should be transferred." In relation to that sentence, did you mean to say, We had informal conversation when we would happen upon General Markac, or did you mean to say General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. It was a slip. I was -- meant to refer to General Markac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you informed us what you meant by paragraph 61. Is there anything there in paragraph 61 right now that you want to change? What you have stated is on record.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially that would be the extent of my correction and should anything else arise, I will correct that during your examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You also said there were two others. Are there any more corrections, or is this it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to make a correction under paragraph 65. Give me a moment, please. In paragraph 65 of the statement, I said that Mr. Markac was there, and I was referring to the general area, specifically somewhere in the area of the village of Ramljane. However, there as it stands now could be understood as at the scene of the event. I heard that General Markac was somewhere in the vicinity of that place at the time when the units were supposed to arrive there, but this general area I was referring to was some ten kilometres away from that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is on record, Mr. Turkalj. What is your last correction?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At paragraph 65, I would like to add that following these assignments - and this is something that isn't in the statement - I spoke to the commander of the action at the time, Mr. Janic, who told me that he had sent -- or, rather, that the unit had completed its assignment and that he had sent it to its base.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that all, Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's another one at paragraph 69. In paragraph 69, I believe I was a bit at cross-purposes with the investigators when it comes to the internal control department. I would like to make a correction in that regard. Within the sector of the special police, there existed the internal control department. However, at the level of the minister, there existed also the office for internal control which dealt with matters of discipline and disciplinary procedure in relation to members of the MUP and special police. Therefore, this department for internal control which was organised within the sector of the special police dealt with the issue of discipline only at the level of statistics that they received regularly from commanders of units or administrations in relation to disciplinary procedures; whereas, the office for internal control dealt more with security issues concerning terrorist groups, matters concerning the manpower and materiel and technical equipment for the special police, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that it, Mr. Turkalj, or are there any further clarifications you would wish to make?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those would roughly be all my corrections of the statement for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now subject to those clarifications, if you were asked the same questions that were asked of you by the members of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2004 and again in 2005 today in court, would your answers be the same, subject to the clarifications that you just provided? And when I say same not verbatim but in terms of substance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, just for clarification, are you specifically only speaking of this statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about this statement at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not any other statement, beyond the one that we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I asked in 2004 and 2005, because 2005 is a video recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Let me see, but you did not ask the witness whether he received the transcript and that he has reviewed that. I think the earlier portion was only about the 2004 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me ask that again, Mr. President. I was under the impression that I did. I will ask him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me first ask you with regard to this statement, Mr. Turkalj. Subject to the clarifications that you provided today, would your responses, if you were asked the same questions that were asked of you in 2004, would your responses be the same substance-wise as reflected in the statement which is in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the answers will be, if not the same, then very similar. I will probably have to be recounting many of these issues from my memory, despite the fact that they are in the statement, and since I have taken the oath, I will, of course, be telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with regard to the transcripts, the witness has testified here that he spoke the truth and the interview was video recorded, so generally we don't go along the same way as we do with a typed written statement. But I could ask him if he has reviewed the transcripts and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we could ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, now you were also provided with the transcripts of your videotaped interview along with the statement; were you not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reviewed the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And is it is, in fact, a videotaped conversation between you and members of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do have you any clarifications to add to that, that can you recall?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reviewed the transcripts, and I don't think that there is any need to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. So if you were asked the questions that were asked of you in 2005 by the members of the Office of the Prosecutor, would you -- would your responses be the same as those reflected in those transcripts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that my answers will be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to move the statement and the transcripts into evidence. The statement is already on the screen. If it may be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from any of the Defence teams. Mr. Registrar, the witness statement dated 3rd and 4th February 2004 would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1149, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P1149 is admitted into evidence. The witness statement dated the 11th March of 2005, which --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There are three 65 ter numbers, Mr. President, between three sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three sections. They could be taken together, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is transcript and video recording attached.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Shall I for the Court give the 65 ter numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They would receive together, Mr. Registrar, which number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1150, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1150 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, your testimony is that you were in charge of the artillery operations of the special police sector in the course of Operation Storm. Now, when you say you were in charge, were you directing all the artillery groups and the batteries attached to all the special police units in the course of the operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I directed the artillery along the axis of attack of the special police, and in one particular battery out of the number you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say "in one particular battery," that is what my question was. Were you directing in one particular battery, or when you say you directed artillery operations to the special police, did you direct the other groups and batteries attached to the other special police units too?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to make a correction. I directed the artillery of the special police with an addition of a -- an attached artillery battery that was in the course of that day attached to the special police forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say an additional artillery battery that was attached, you're referring to the HV battery that was attached for the purpose of the operation to the special police, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was platoon from the HV. There was a gun platoon that was attached to us, a Howitzer platoon as well as a multi-barrel rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have -- now prior to the commencement of the operation, did you receive a list of targets which were to be engaged in the course of the operation either from Mr. Markac or Mr. Sacic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A list of targets and potential targets is what I received from the employees of the internal control department.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what were those targets, if you could recall?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The targets were along the front line of the enemy defence as well as certain targets in depth behind their lines, command points, railroad junctions, warehouses of equipment and pieces, communications centre. That would be it more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were those instructions given in writing?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were clearly designated by the department.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where would those lists be archived now, do you know, since you're still in the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't provide an answer to that. I don't know whether such lists exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at any stage as the person in charge of artillery, did you send this list to either Mr. Markac or the chief of the sector, Mr. Sacic, for their approval, or did they get involved in the planning of the artillery operations with you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The artillery operation and the targets we engaged fell under my authority. Since Mr. Sacic was at the head of the staff of the special police forces, I advised him of the targets, but that did not mean that he necessarily needed to know where each particular target was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, along with this list of targets that you received, did you receive any information from the inner control branch or any other department regarding the presence or absence of civilians close to those targets that you were supposed to engaged [sic]?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once we received the targets, we still had no information as to any civilians in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, you say: We still had no information as to the civilians in that area. Is that your information were that there were -- when civilians or that you did not receive any information regarding civilians? It's not very clear. Can you clarify what you just said.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information on the military targets in that area, given the tasks which had been assigned to us in the course of an attack during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. Now, my question was: Did you have the any information of the proximity of civilians or civilian settlements to those targets?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent I could see how close the civilian settlements were to the targets themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you clarify that answer. What do you mean you could see? You knew that there were civilian settlements close to the targets. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you are misrepresenting the answer of the witness. The witness said to a certain extent, I could see how close the civilian settlements were to the targets themselves. Your question gave a different version, although using the same words.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I did not intend to misrepresent, I read it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I -- you put the question to the witness again. Although is it by visual observation that you saw that, Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not by visual observation. I could see it on the map. I could see clearly where each and every target in the area was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now perhaps just to -- you received maps. The targets were indicated on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received a map of the area that had been charted by the internal control department with certain information. I was the one to determine which targets were to be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the map that was provided to you by internal control department, did that map -- what were the military targets [indiscernible] in that map?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a topographic map of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And my question was were the -- the military targets indicated depicted in that map that was given to you by the inner control branch?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat, that it was a topographic map of that area, with all roads and facilities marked. As for the targets, that is to say the information received from the internal control department as to the exact lotion of the targets, we used that to plot the targets. Perhaps I can clarify. If a target was a cross-roads, and if it was presumed that new fresh forces were being brought in through that juncture, then I designated that as a target.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you received -- when you listed out the targets, about -- approximately how many targets did you end up with as targets to be engaged in the course of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a really broad question. Targets where and at a what point in time. It is so expansive. If it could be more specific, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We certainly will have to come to more specifics, Ms. Mahindaratne. If you have already in your mind where to go then --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... perhaps there's a quicker way of going there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to answer my question?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. But I can't tell you what the exact number of targets was. There were many of them along the front line and then in the back. There may have been over 100 targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, well, I'll come to this later on, Mr. Turkalj, I think we'll go area an area, and I'm no more interested in the targets in the area behind the front lines, in the depth. But can you tell me before we close for the day what were the rules of engagement that you received in planning your artillery operation, particularly with regard to engaging targets in the proximity of civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a very comprehensive question. It would probably take a while for me to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Did you receive such instructions, either from Mr. Markac or Mr. Sacic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received instructions from Mr. Sacic in the sense that artillery support was to be provided to the special police forces along our axis of attack. We all knew what the axis of movement were, that is to say the main axis of attack and auxiliary lines of attack of the special police forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You misunderstood me. My question is what were the rules of engagement as in were you informed as to what you could target, what you could not, and in selecting particular targets, what kind of precautionary methods you should take, that's what I mean. Rules of engagement. Did you have rules of engagement in considering artillery operations, within the special police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no rules of engagement for artillery per se. What we had in place was the tactics of artillery, based on which we acted upon in the course of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you note the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Turkalj, we will adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning in Courtroom I, and I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether it is the testimony you gave already, or whether it is testimony still to be given. And may I further invite you during your examination to refrain from seeking eye contact with others and focus on Ms. Mahindaratne or, at a later stage, the one who examines you, to focus on that. We stand adjourned, and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 12th of December, 9.00, Courtroom I.
